utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, General Galic, everyone in this courtroom. Before we continue with the cross-examination of the witness Kupusovic, I'd like to give you the decision on the objection made by the Prosecution yesterday on the exhibit, a few lines, two lines from a book of Stjepan Siber, the lines indicating that sniper rifles would have been distributed. But before giving the decision, I would just like to make a few short remarks on the law of evidence to be practised in this Court. As we all know, this is a mixed Court to the extent that not common-law traditions nor civil law traditions will apply. And I may bring into your mind that one of the main features of the common-law tradition as far as the law of evidence is concerned is that they mainly deal with rules of presentation of evidence, while in the civil law tradition, the emphasis is on the evaluation of the evidential material that is available to the Court. And if we look at the rationale behind the rules of evidence, and perhaps a bit more in the common-law tradition as it is in the civil law tradition, we will see that one of the rationale is that the mistrust of juries, where there might be some fear that a jury might not be able to properly evaluate some kind of evidence that is presented to it. You will understand that this fear is a bit less in this Court since there is no jury, and the Court thinks that, like in most civil law traditions, as professional Judges, we will be able to evaluate properly the evidence that is presented before us. The second rationale is the fact finding which, of course, is of major importance, and a third, and not the least important for this Court - of course, I'm not going through all the rationales, but those that seem to be of importance at this moment - is to control the scope and the duration of the trials. That's a very pragmatic rationale, but it is still important to this Court. Bearing this in mind, we have considered what to do with the two lines all of the book of Stjepan Siber. We then considered Rule 89, paragraph (c), which says the Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. In view of the testimony of the witness Kupusovic, the Chamber thinks that the two lines of the book contain no relevant evidence and that these two lines have no probative value. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, I clarify this position. If the Defence would in a later stage want to establish that sniper rifles have been distributed, of course they can do -- they can adduce whatever kind of evidence in order to support that idea. But at this moment, in view of this testimony, this Court thinks that it would be inadmissible evidence to accept these lines of the book of Mr. Stjepan Siber. I told you that the control of the scope and the duration of trials is of importance to this Court as well, and we want to avoid that every newspaper article, every book that a witness has not read is tendered into evidence because we will end up with a lot of paper, which might not serve the Court in coming to conclusions. The Defence has argued that the witness could not just deny what was in the book. This is not a reason to admit this book in evidence, because whether it's true or not, what is in the book, or whether the witness is telling the truth or not when he says, "I didn't know anything about what is written in this book," this is not a way of establishing what is the truth in that respect. So that would be no reason to admit these lines of the book into evidence. So that's the decision of this Chamber on this objection. Then I'd like the witness to be brought into the Court. Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, whilst the witness is being brought in, might I raise a procedural matter indirectly arising from your ruling, and it is this: Not having appeared in a trial here before, I'm uncertain as to whether the Trial Chamber has a system whereby items shown to a witness but not tendered at that stage can be marked for identification so there can be no doubt at a later stage whether it is tendered, that it is the same item that was shown to an earlier witness. I would be grateful for your clarification on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it is not my first trial, having a certain history in this Court, I'd rather discuss this with my colleagues first before I give you a final answer to that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kupusovic. May I remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind I that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made the day before yesterday, and I will give an opportunity now to Ms. Pilipovic to continue cross-examination. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were discussing the shortage of electricity, water, and gas in Sarajevo while you were a member of the War Presidency. Tell me, please, do you have any knowledge to the effect that the main transformer station to the electricity was in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 11 transformer stations in Sarajevo, so in addition to the one in Hadzici, there were another 10 transformer stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that transformer station connected to the water source at Ilidza, at Bacevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transformer station in Blazuj was linked to that source of water in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area where the transformer station in Blazuj was, who controlled the area?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Karadzic's Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that that transformer station during operations by the BH army and the army of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was damaged?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any direct knowledge, only from the stories in town that there may have been damages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of that, if it was damaged, does that mean that the Bacevo water source was not operational?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends, of course, to what extent it was damaged because it is a large transformer station and it applies not only Bacevo but that part of the town of Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were active in the War Presidency, you said that you went to attend negotiations when there was a shortage of water and electricity. Who was present and were any of the UN observers present?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the Presidency of the city, I participated several times in those negotiations which were conducted by representatives of the UN as independent observers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to visit the scene where these things were actually happening?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, members of the commission did not visit the spot. This was not allowed by the negotiators on the opposite side, but they did go -- workers went there who could, together with the workers of the other side, under UN supervision, repair whatever damage had occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were active, did you know what was happening and whether there was a shortage of electricity and water in the part of the town that was under the control of the army of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would happen that part of town at Grbavica and the rest of the city to be left without electricity, but frequently also Vrace and Grbavica had electricity whereas the main part of town under the control of the legal authorities in Sarajevo had no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you deal with that situation then?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there would be negotiations at the airport on the conditions under which electricity would be allowed to reach the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were performing those duties prior to becoming town mayor, what other duties did you have, or rather all of you who were active in that War Presidency? I am referring to questions of food, clothing, and accommodation of both civilians and the military.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the city had responsibilities that were parallel to those of the Municipal Assembly, which meant the highest legislative body in the city of Sarajevo. Therefore, in addition to questions of water and electricity, we were also involved with the other ten or so public services that are normally operating in town, transportation, garbage disposal, burials, marketplaces, and so on. We had a commission for the distribution of humanitarian aid which regularly reported to us, and it was directly linked to representatives of the UNHRC, who took care of the delivery and distribution of humanitarian aid by district, whereas our responsibilities were limited to the local level, that is distribution among families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you also concerned yourself with the food, accommodation and clothing of the army?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as the city Presidency, we had nothing to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took care of that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence and the army command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, in the course of your activities, did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you have any knowledge that within the territory of the city of Sarajevo there were prisons?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of the city of Sarajevo before the war, during the war, and even today, there is the so-called central penitentiary, which is situated next to the main court. And as far as I know, it was operating throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a prison in the Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at Dobrinja in the coffee bar Sunce, which used to be a coffee bar, was also a prison?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information that in the territory of Sarajevo, there were 46 prisons and these were prisons for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly no prisons for Serbs, but Pale television frequently spoke about a prison at Zetra, that is the Olympic sports hall, that I know for certain did not exist at all because my working place was right close to Zetra, and Zetra was in fact empty. And later it was a warehouse for UNHCR humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to that sports hall?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there a couple of times, accompanied by representatives of the UNHCR when they wanted to show us what aid had arrived. And this is two levels below the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this? Was this when you were a member of the war Presidency or when you became town mayor?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the course of 1993, while I was a member of the town presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you moved around on a daily basis, that you went to work. When you moved around town, did you ever attend or see a victim of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and I didn't move around town every day, as that was impossible. Frequently, the shelling and sniping was of such intensity that we didn't venture out of the basements. And quite frequently, 10 or 20 metres behind me or in front of me, I would see casualties of the shooting, that is of sniping or of a shell. And I myself was twice in great danger because a shell exploded on the balcony just above my head, but the shrapnel entered the city. Lucky for me, but unfortunately for the inhabitants because they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything about it? Did you inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing we did was to flee for shelter. And in this particular case that I mentioned, it happened in June 1992. And the next day or the day after, when things calmed down, then we tried to intervene with the UN forces in Sarajevo to bring their influence to bear on the other side to cease shelling of civilians because this is something they also witnessed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that they also witnessed this. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were accommodated in Skenderija when the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated there. So in several locations in town, they had their centres, and they often moved around town in APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the procedure was when someone was wounded in the street? Who took care of them and where were those people driven or transported?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently, whoever arrived first in a car would pick up the casualty and drive him or her to the closest clinic or hospital. And normally, it was the emergency service. But often one couldn't wait for the emergency service to arrive. But anyone who would come by in a car or in some other way would carry or transport the wounded person to the nearest clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the highest buildings in the centre of Sarajevo, such as the building of the executive council or government, the Oslobodjenje building and other high rises, that there were snipers on those buildings?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have knowledge that there were anti-sniper teams of UN forces on those buildings which we frequently called on, and then those anti-sniping teams were formed to respond to sniping from Vrace. And indeed, for a time they were positioned on the highest buildings of the government, Energoinvest, and the Unis skyscrapers. But as they, too, were killed by snipers, the French UNPROFOR command later withdrew them. So these were not sniper -- snipers belonging to the army or the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but rather anti-sniping teams belonging to the UN forces, which were supposed to repel the snipers from the lines of the siege of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common knowledge in Sarajevo, actually. I didn't actually see those soldiers because they were positioned behind barriers, shelters, on those top floors. But there were conversations that I did not participate in directly because that was done by the town mayor at the time, together with the commander of the UN forces in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with the town mayor and did you brief him on behalf of your War Presidency about events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings of the city Presidency were held as a rule once a week, sometimes more frequently. And at times when -- if on the day of the meeting there was heavy shelling, then the following day, the meeting was held. These meetings were chaired by the town mayor, Kresin Jakovic [phoen], and we had a prepared agenda, and all topical matters that had occurred a day or two before or were expected to occur in the next few days were reviewed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that AS, anti-snipers, UN observers were set up. When was that? What year, what month?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in the autumn of 1993, and this went on for several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that in a part of Sarajevo -- when I say a part of Sarajevo, I mean the urban part of town. Do you know whether any special sniper units existed under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the civilian casualties, do you consider that Sarajevo as a united town, not only the urban part but the whole of the city of Sarajevo, that civilians fell as casualties in the whole of the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the civilians were casualties all over the city, but you cannot compare the civilian casualties in the surrounding parts of the town under the control of Karadzic's Serbs, the army of Karadzic's Serbs, and the civilians in the town of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, do you mean that the Grbavica neighbourhood, that there were less casualties there than in the part of Sarajevo that borders on the Grbavica district, or was it the same on both sides?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many civilians were killed at Grbavica, but probably they were killed and wounded, but they were all -- also fell as casualties because they had no water and electricity and so on. Their life was constantly threatened due to the effects of war and the suffering war brings with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the citizens of Sarajevo living at Grbavica, did they fall casualty from shelling and sniping during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know how many fell as casualties, but I say they could have been killed because, quite simply, the demarcation line was the Mijetska River, so in this part of town where I moved around in, it was obvious with the skyrises and with all the buildings on that side, that people had evacuated them. It was not possible to live there because the soldiers belonging to the army of Republica Sprska had taken them over. And on the other side in similar buildings, in similar highrises, the situation was similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to Grbavica when you say highrises?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm thinking of the building like the BH assembly building, the electricity board on the other side of the Mijetska River which was controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the situation in Nedzarici, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzarici is, in fact, a village which became an urban part of town as the town expanded. And on the 2nd of May, when the war began in Sarajevo and the fighting, it became a stronghold, a bunker, for sniping and shelling of the road leading from the Oslobodjenje building towards Dobrinja and that settlement is on the right-hand side of that road. The civilians who were of non-Serb ethnicity were taken away in an unknown direction or some of them were transferred to town. And they said that they had been forced to flee there by the extremist Serbs. Now, what happened to the civilians living in Nedzarici, I really want say. I don't know. I mean the Serb civilians, I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to visit that particular settlement, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several months after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the impression you gained?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of damaged and destroyed houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that in that settlement, the houses are mostly two-storey buildings?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one floor or two floors, family-type dwellings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the district surrounded by high buildings of Vojnicko Polje, and Ali Pasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one side of the district, there are the high buildings of Vojnicko Polje, yes. And they are in the same state they were in during the war, that is to say, snipers and grenades hit the buildings so they have these marks on them from the Nedzarici area, so those skyrises were left first, were evacuated first on the 2nd of May when the war and the fighting started. On the other side, there is the JNA barracks in Nedzarici which became barracks of the army of Republika Srpska, and on the third side is the airport, the beginning of the runway, in fact. On the eastern side lies the Oslobodjenje newspaper building, and it was targeted from Nedzarici and has been largely destroyed and still stands like that. It hasn't been restored or rebuilt yet. And that is 200 metres away from the Nedzarici settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Ali Pasino Polje and Nedzarici separated by a road? Does a road separate the two?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side we had the Vojnicko Polje settlement and the health centre in Nedzarici. And in Vojnicko Polje, actually, which was built when Vojnicko Polje was built and that was completely destroyed with the first shootings from Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that during the war in that part of town were the demarcation lines, the separation lines, and that these ran for 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the demarcation line was for all practical purposes that road because from Ali Pasino Polje on the other side, the situation was already like it was in town. So just the buildings that were hidden by the Vojnicko Polje area. And you asked me about 50 metres, well, I can't really say. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at Ali Pasino Polje, military facilities had been set up in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first buildings, or rather, the accompanying facilities were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evacuated straight away on the 2nd of May. Nobody could survive because from Nedzarici, there was shooting. Soldiers shot from there, and others. And only later on when the lines were established, the BH army was certainly there. But I have no direct knowledge as to which locality they were in in Nedzarici. There was quite a lot of frequent fighting along that line with Nedzarici on the one side and the road and the hillocks and slopes on the other side of Ali Posina Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who destroyed the buildings and facilities in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably destroyed during the fighting. I don't know who but probably during the fighting, the buildings were damaged and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how frequent the fighting was? Was there fighting on a daily basis or sporadic fighting?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from time to time there was fighting but, very often, in Nedzarici there was fighting because the front lines were close by. And it was an effort to link up Dobrinja with the town with a more secure road, so that those first houses in Nedzarici which were facing the roads towards Dobrinja were practically completely destroyed. And this could be seen later on when the road became more secure and safer because the army of Republika Srpska, which was in Nedzarici, was expelled from those first houses. They had to withdraw from those first houses. So the army didn't take them over. It was just in this sort of demarcation area or line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of Dobrinja was to have been linked up with the town, because you said 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the whole of Dobrinja, the part under the control of Republika Srpska, which is 5 or 10 percent, several buildings boarding on the Lukavica barracks, which quite recently joined to Dobrinja. So this is one settlement with all these different phases which got their name as they were built. But otherwise, 40.000 Sarajevo inhabitants lived in the Dobrinja district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, the fighting took place for Dobrinja 1, 2, 3 and 4 to be linked up with the urban part of town, as you call it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the communication between Dobrinja by road to Ali Pasino Polje was enabled. So Dobrinja until that withdrawal of the army of Republika Srpska from the first front-line houses in Nedzarici controlled the road. And Dobrinja was in a double encirclement. There was the siege around the whole of the city, and then Dobrinja was under siege -- a siege of its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, how many Serbs there were in Sarajevo before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you, yourself, were the mayor, how many of them were there when you were town mayor?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assessment was that there were between 40.000 to 50.000 Serbs, and these were assessments by the Serb citizens council. No census, no population census was taken during the war but I think the assessments and evaluations were correct, at least judging by the lists of humanitarian AID organisations and the lists of citizens receiving humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs are there in Sarajevo today?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably 70.000, 80.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you get your figures from, what sources?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to today's figure, it is a figure that appears in the media from time to time. But nobody knows the exact figure until a census is conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the media, do you mean the media in Sarajevo or the media further afield?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media that work in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo and further afield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, was -- were the media functioning?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The paper Oslobodjenje came out every day. The radio was working all the time. Television, in part, during the day. And there were other newspapers, too, that were published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who the director of the Oslobodjenje newspaper was and who published the paper, who printed it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The publishing house Oslobodjenje published the paper, and their director was, I think, Mr. Hasan Asengic [phoen] or some such name, who had been the director before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the prosecuting team whether there's any need of re-examination on those subjects that have been touched by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. We will not avail ourselves of re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Kupusovic, this is the end of your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, and you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, as I indicated yesterday, we would have a short status conference now, but since the courtroom has to be prepared for that, I would like to have a short break. Let's say ... I understand that it takes 30 minutes to change the courtroom, so perhaps it would be wise to see whether we can do it in a more efficient way. Perhaps one question without violating any confidentiality. We had spoken yesterday about the possible withdrawal of a motion. Could you, without giving any further details, could the Prosecution please tell us whether the motion I was just referring to will be withdrawn or not, without going in any details because I know it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then I shall give an undetailed reply. Mr. President. Yes, we will seek to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This also means that there might be -- but I'm also looking to the Defence that there might be no problem in perhaps continuing at this moment with the next witness, and do the status conference later on, unless this would cause you problems -- perhaps we can't finish it today. Perhaps instead of having a formal status conference, perhaps we'll turn into, as far as I understand, a private session so that we can discuss the matters we intended to discuss during the status conference. If all parties agree, if there's no objection, I'll then now change to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we in private session now or -- just for a moment, please. After consulting with colleagues, we decided that we would discuss the matters in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday, one of the things I asked the parties to inform the Chamber about any recent exchange of documents and the disclosure. We have not received information on that as far as I'm aware of. Just before discussing the issue, I would like to ask the Defence whether they have any factual information on recent disclosure, and I would do the same to the Prosecution. Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor on this precise question about recent communications of files or information. I've got nothing to signal in particular. I'm talking about recent communications, but I wish once again to express myself on matters of principle connected with all the problems which have been mooted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give you an opportunity for that later on. Mr. Ierace, is there any -- because I got the impression yesterday that there had been some recent disclosure or exchange of documents. Could you please inform the Chamber about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. To remind you of what Mr. Piletta-Zanin said yesterday, he informed the Trial Chamber that a few hours before he rose to his feet, that he had received 97 folders, and I think he later corrected that to 87 folders. The situation is that, in fact, on the 1st of December, not yesterday, the Prosecution delivered to the Defence in the form of Ms. Pilipovic 68 binders of documents. They were delivered at two times on Saturday, the 1st of December, the first at around 3.30 in the afternoon, and the second at around 5.00 the same afternoon. And they were delivered personally to Ms. Pilipovic and an assistant who was with her at the time. Mr. President, those 68 binders represent the documentary entries in the amended exhibit list, with these exceptions: That there are some documents that we are still locating, approximately 190, and there are some documents in relation to which we still await Rule 70 clearance from various bodies, and other procedures to be carried out. I can indicate in more detail those numbers. In relation to documents for which we are awaiting Rule 70 clearance, there are 591 -- I'm sorry, 619, and 591 have recently been cleared by New York and have been provided to the Defence on the weekend. There are some other smaller number of documents which require Rule 70 clearance. And I don't know that we need to go through those at this stage. Those are by far the largest number and the biggest bundle. That is the only recent disclosure, that is, in the last few days, that I'm aware of, Mr. President. I can also indicate beyond that, if you wish me to address matters more broadly, that the Prosecution is continuing to check and recheck the documentation which it wishes to disclose to the Defence and which it is obliged to disclose to the Defence to ensure that both those categories are satisfied. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, will you please respond to the remarks of the Prosecution and to bring to the attention of the Chamber whatever you want in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I will answer, also expound, if you will let me, the very great concern of the Defence for this. As a concrete example, numbering of the exhibits. I had to refer to the Registry, ask the Registry because we didn't know how to number them because we didn't know if an exhibit was going to be accepted or rejected by your Chamber. This is the reason why they will not always be a numbering on the exhibits which I will now present. It's a very small detail, but accumulated with others it may become important. What I wish to say here is we received from the Prosecution about 10 metres in line of bundles for the Defence, and I heard Mr. Ierace say that these exhibits were essential to these proceedings, whether they contain this or that fact, which might be reproached to General Galic. I think I heard also that the exhibits were admitted during the weekend, on the 1st of December. I was in The Hague. I didn't have materially the time to peruse 50.000 pages, I think. And for this, I wish to thank the Prosecution: We were given a search engine which is part of the computer system. And I think your Tribunal probably will be interested to know about it also. The first two exhibits which I wish to tender are nothing else but the printer exhibits, as it has been communicated by the Prosecution, with numbers D/3 and D/4 as the Registry requested me to number them. Now, may I now transmit them to your office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are they in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent question, Mr. President. I will answer immediately. Partly in extraterrestrial language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a language I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My third ear either, Mr. President. But it is with pleasure I will show them and bring them to you. I should think that if everybody has got the exhibits, we could start by Exhibit D/3, Mr. President. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document, which you are now seeing is a just a photography -- a photograph of what appears when the Prosecution search engine works. You just type key "S" for the Defence to see what is recognised by the search engine on the computer, and you will find under letter "S" things which are totally unreal. I would like to ask Mr. Ierace what is meant SY3W -- see, I don't think he speaks extraterrestrial either. I will not go further. What I mean to say, Mr. President, is that the means we have at hand are not technically reliable because the action is we have got names which are hidden here. It might seem a joke, but it's not a joke, because if we pass upon that very quickly on the indictment, and we take the next number, if you will, D/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will allow me, Mr. Counsel, I'm taking it quite seriously what you say, and I've got only one answer to that: Never search for "S" as such, because you might get every combination that has an "S" in it, whether it's useful or not. So I would say that this is hardly a demonstration, whether it works or not. I am quite interested to see whether this is of any use to you, but not by searching an "S." So I would leave out discussion on a search performed just on the letter "S," because that's what -- not only what you get but what you can expect to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for your observation. Thank you so much. You are perfectly right, perfectly right. But simply what I wish to say - and I can demonstrate it with a witness, if need be - is that if the computer reads that sort of things, there are names hidden behind these codes. I can follow your thought, underlying thought. But if I make another research, and if I, for instance, type "Galic," which is the only thing I'm interested in, the name Galic, the indicted, and Taljanic, in practice. I don't think I will be reproached for any mistake -- from doing any mistake. I see that the research doesn't yield any result. But I would like to call the attention of your Chamber to the fact that I didn't present this exhibit, but it is one of the exhibits tendered by the prosecution, which is called "The Battle of Sarajevo." I will give the computer references later, in which these two names may be found, Galic and Taljanic. But you have the proof that the result of the search gives 0, yields 0. If you want to try it, if you have the disks, pages 7 and 11 of document entitled "Battle of Sarajevo" - maybe the Prosecution can produce it while I'm talking - well, you will find these occurrences Galic and Taljanic. What I want to demonstrate by the exercise which you yourself -- I'll ask you not to only type "S" to have results, but if I type "Galic," something else, we get no result at all. And I have the documents here. I can tender it to you. There are some documents with these occurrences. We can, therefore, not work on a such a basis. And I only received after Saturday, at the beginning of the week, these perhaps 68, 70, 80 bundles with a search engine which does not, will not function. It is true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would allow me to interrupt as well. I don't think that in this courtroom we can spend a lot of time on discussing whether a certain search engine does work or not. I'm quite sure that the Prosecution, who has provided you with this search engine, will be of help to see whether it can be useful for you or not. Perhaps one of the Prosecution assistants could give some assistance to the Defence in how to use it, because it could make a lot of remarks on how Galic and Taljanic would work as a search statement. But this is not the place to discuss these kind of things. Would the Prosecution, if there's any problem in using this instrument or giving some education in it, would it be somewhat available to help the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, that search engine was first provided many months ago to the Defence on a CD, on a number of CDs with documents which we disclosed. It has not been provided with documents which we have placed on the exhibit list, except insofar as they were previously closed. At the outset when it was provided, the Defence was invited to contact us, if they wanted some assistance in operating the search engine. The first complaint that I heard in relation to it was last Thursday, when I met up with Mr. Piletta-Zanin in my office. He said he had a problem. I immediately offered him the assistance of the OTP to explain to him how Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the search engine worked, and he said he didn't want it. He then asked me if he could have a hard copy of the exhibit list. I told him he could have it the next day. And he said that he -- it didn't suit him to have the hard copy the next day, so I said, "Well, let us know when you want and where you want it, and we'll give it to you." And that's what we did on Saturday. The Office of the Prosecutor remains available to assist my friends to search those documents. There is one further point I would make: Disclosure, that is, reciprocal disclosure, comes under Rule 66(B). That only requires the Office of the Prosecutor to make available the books, documents, and so on for inspection. The Office of the Prosecutor chose to go beyond that and to give copies of the documents to the Defence. They told us what categories they wanted. We provided them. We provided them on CD with a search engine. So in my respectful submission, this complaint has to be seen in context. We have disclosed since the 9th of January 6.236, approximately, documents. It seems sensible to us, since we were providing what they asked for, that if we had a search engine, we should give them that as well with an offer of assistance, and that's what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I think we have to establish that for one reason or another, Mr. Piletta-Zanin is at this moment not able to achieve the results he would like to have with the search engine, but on the other hand also that all possibilities to use this engine perhaps better have not been exhausted yet. So I would like to leave the issue of the search engine at this moment. We've taken notice of the complaints of Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and I would invite him to bring other issues to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President. Yes, of course. Thank you for your consideration. Yes, I worked with very good teams computer-wise, and I have to say -- with all respect, I have -- all due respect, you have several scanning systems, and this is what happens when a page is presented, willfully or not, the other way around, whatever technician, in particular those who tried to help me, the scan which is used does not manage to read the words. It is not a matter of competence of the members of the Prosecution or Defence. It's a matter of procedure. If a page is put upside down, the scan will not recognise the words. And by this rather clever ways, sometimes that's the reality, all you need to do is to put a page upside down and the result would be precisely what you've got in D/3, this accumulation of names which don't mean anything. And if there are so many names, it's because some pages were put in the machine upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to interrupt you again, I think that I consider the issue that you are bringing to the attention of the Chamber now also deals with the search engine, possibility of the search engines, and I think that I had decided that this discussion would, for the moment, be over. And I have taken note of this. This Chamber has taken note that you don't think at this moment that you can have any use of it, and it doesn't work for you. So if there's any other issue on the exchange, disclosure of documents, you would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Just one. I will not come back to this question of the search engine, which is perfectly clear. I think I heard the Chamber say a moment ago that we should tender only pertinent documents, and the search engine produced this sort of document, Mr. President, which I have to bring to the attention of your Chamber because I think it is not with this that you can prove or disprove anything. It's a document under the 06051 produced by the search engine, and it's an article with some press caricatures, and which has nothing to do with this procedure. What I mean to say here is we have an enormous quantity, amount of these kind of documents. The defence is not able to sort them out with a competent or not search engine. It is not for us actually to sort these things out. This is number 25. But those are produced by the Prosecution. And to finish this, I wish to thank the Chamber for listening to me on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other issue about the disclosure or exchange of documents that hasn't been discussed at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps a last point, Mr. President, to be examined, very last point. We'll use it -- we'll give an example for one exhibit which has been tendered by the Prosecution and which without a search engine gives two different numbers, serial numbers. I don't know which to take first. I've got number 00268208, 00361575. May I repeat these numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just look at the screen whether the numbers are written down properly. I think the first number is not correctly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will say again, the two numbers of these exhibits. The first I quoted was 00268208, and the other document, the other number was 00361575. I made copies if need be, which I could tender. That one can see the problem even from where you are sitting, Defence can strictly not take anything useful out of a document which is mostly illegible, and this is one of the reasons why the search engine doesn't work. We have there a document which gives an example, a clear example, that it is not possible to make any use of it. I will deposit it as Exhibit D/6, so it can be seen but technical and human difficulties which is -- the Defence is confronted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the D/6 document is concerned, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you ask the Prosecution for a better copy, a copy you could read?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, but I have to specify that this has to do with about 60 folders, and this is only one example of an incredible number of documents which all appear in this state. I really do not have the means of reading them. I'm very sorry, we can't work that way. It's not workable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Would the Prosecution respond to that, briefly if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President. In relation to the latter of the two documents, that is the medical report, firstly, I note that although I cannot read B/C/S, I can see most of the letters which are on that document. Secondly, I make this observation, that the Defence informed the Prosecution, I think now some three months ago, that they were having difficulty in reading some of the photocopies of the medical reports, and we agreed with him that some parts of the medical reports were illegible, and we would take steps to obtain better copies. With that in mind, we undertook a special mission to Sarajevo to get the best possible copies of the medical reports we could, and they were brought back to The Hague in October, and within days of receiving them here, we disclosed them to the Defence. It may be that this is one of those documents. I don't say that we now have a set of medical records where every single one of them is 100 percent legible, but I do say we have the most legible set possible. And nothing more can be done about that. I come now to the first document which appears to be an article from the Chicago Tribune with a political cartoon beneath it. I note that my friend said this was off the exhibit list. He's given us two numbers. I would be grateful if he could give us the tracking number for this exhibit so that I can make some inquiries and enlighten the Trial Chamber as to why it is on the exhibit list, if indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just comment shortly on it. This Chamber is very well aware of the problems the Defence has in let me say digesting the huge number of documents they received. This Chamber also is of the view that we should try to solve the problems related to it and not to exploit the problems as such. So whenever there's a problem, I would call upon the parties first to communicate to each other to see whether they can solve the problem. And at the same time, I can tell you that until a decision has been taken on the leave for appeal that has been filed by the Prosecution against the decision of the 16th of November of the Pre-Trial Judge concerning the admissibility of documents, this Trial Chamber is -- has the intention not to allow any surprise disclosure of documents, the use of documents by surprise. So I would ask the Prosecution that if at this moment they can foresee what documents should be studied by priority, because they are produced on a short notice, that at least they will inform the Defence about it so that they can prepare as good as they can. If, on the other hand, the Defence is confronted with a document of which they think they have not been able to prepare properly, the Defence can just tell the Trial Chamber and we'll look into the matter and see what solution, if there is one, can be found. This is a call -- I'm calling upon both parties to see whether they can work as efficiently as possible. I would finally give both parties one possibility to react on what I have just said. If you agree, it's fine. If you disagree, please tell us briefly why. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, thank you for what you just said. And Defence has already had an opportunity to say what it has repeated and will repeat again to your Chamber in its other composition. Let me just say that the essential will of the Defence was to find the truth, and in particular, the will of the Defence is to help justice, to be the facilitator of justice, and nothing else. But in this connection, as a barrister, I think I can recognise perhaps as a computer expert, to recognize the problems. We will do all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we can to try and limit these problems but in this phase we can't do anything else but to respectfully invite the Prosecution to eliminate from its case file documents such as those which we have presented today, and which apparently will not be readable and will not be reproduced before we don't know how much time. So let us eliminate these documents. I said yesterday that only 37 documents contained the name of General Galic, only 37 documents out of perhaps 40.000 pages or more, perhaps. Let us make an effort in the name of justice, in the name of the clarity of the debate, I invite my colleagues, and I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything the Prosecution want to say about this, just also as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will keep it very brief, Mr. President. In relation to reciprocal disclosure, I regret that the Defence did not tell us six months ago that all they wanted were documents that mentioned the name Galic. In relation to making exhibits available to the Defence in advance, there is only one witness we who will be calling in the next four days through whom exhibits will be tendered, and that is the Witness Mr. Nakas. Copies of those exhibits, although they were disclosed many, many months ago, will be deposited in the Defence locker this afternoon. Mr. President, the only other issue I would raise in relation to disclosure relates to reciprocal disclosure of documents by the Defence. Mrs. Pilipovic has told me, I think now some six weeks ago, that the Defence has not yet completed its obligation to disclose documents to the Prosecution, and I would be grateful if she could give some indication as to when that process is likely to be completed. I have some understanding of the difficulties which are involved with disclosure. This is by far the most extensive reciprocal trial that the Tribunal has dealt with, and it has posed enormous problems. But nevertheless I would be grateful if she could provide a date or a month by which she will have given us all of the documents of which she is presently aware, which come under reciprocal disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that both parties are willing to assist each other and fully comprehend the problems the parties are facing at this moment. I think we discussed at this moment the issue of disclosure of documents in general. Whenever there comes a point when someone is surprised by any document, please let the Chamber know immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just say I found there to be a very cooperative atmosphere with the Defence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is good to hear, Mr. Ierace. Then I would like to proceed. Let me just have a look at the clock. I think it is still useful to start the examination of your witness, Mr. Ierace. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would be convenient to the Prosecution, Mr. President. Mr. Blaxill will take the next witness. Will you allow us to make some changes at the bar table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the documents that have just been provided by the Defence should be admitted. Whether they have any value for -- any probative value is a different matter, but I think they have played a role in our discussion. Therefore, they should be registered properly. So with the consent of both parties as I hope, they will be registered, get a number, and -- well, admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit numbers will be D/3, D/4, D/5, and D/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. With the Court's indulgence, my learned colleague Mark mentioned the introduction of documents through a witness. For us to be as effective as possible and for the Defence to state its views as to those documents, I should like to ask my learned colleagues if they could at least tell us two days in advance so that the Defence knows which documents they are. My colleagues tell me that they have been disclosed. I can't say at this point in time, so I would like to ask them to supply us with those documents at least two days before the witness is due to come on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I can see on these newest lists, exhibits are mentioned. So if these lists are communicated to the Defence, I think you may be aware, but it's your intention to communicate these lists to the Defence so that you know up until -- well, let's say the 14th witness, what exhibits the Prosecution intends to tender, and they have offered to put in your mail box this afternoon those documents that will be tendered in evidence for the coming days. Okay, then. I think we can proceed with the examination of the next witness, which is not a witness under pseudonym. Mr. Ierace, your next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac. Could the usher please bring in the witness. It is suggested by the Registry that we have the break now, and then perhaps continue. I'm asking the interpreters booth whether if we continue at 20 minutes to 6.00, whether we could continue until 7.00. Would this be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we better have a break now for 20 minutes, and then continue until 7.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's already for the third time today I asked the Prosecution who they will call as their next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. It will be Mr. Mustafa Kovac who we will call to testify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please bring in the witness. I just ask the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Kovac, can you hear me in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, Rule 90(A) requires you to make a solemn declaration, of which the text will be provided to you. And I invite you to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I am much obliged to you, Mr. President. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac. Would you please give the Court your full name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is a problem, as far as the audio is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, would you be so kind as to give your full name and your date of birth to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: My name is Mustafa Kovac. I was born on the 12th of March, 1958 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, are you a married man?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: I have three children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all three of your children alive in 1992? They had all been born by then, had they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Chamber briefly about your educational background. What education did you follow?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Sarajevo. It was the Blagoje Parovic primary school. And then I graduated from the 3rd gymnasium in Sarajevo and then went on to the Faculty of Political Sciences. It was the Veljko Vlahovic faculty in Sarajevo. And at present, I am doing post-graduate studies. My thesis is in the field of Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your education, did you do any compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: That was in 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in what military disciplines or activities were you trained?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: I was trained as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any other kind of training in the use of particular weapons or any kind of particular skills?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Only within the frameworks of general military training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would those frameworks have included?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslav People's Army, there was specialised training linked to training for military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, did that include any form of weapon training?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We were taught marksmanship, and as soldiers, we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did marksmanship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you issued any equipment for that specific purpose? Personally, that is.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you actually issued with so you could do that basic training?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: As far as basic training was concerned, we were issued weapons, and I got a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to a sniper rifle, what sort of thing is that, please? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It is a type of weapon that the military police used in the execution of its duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any difference between a sniper rifle -- I do beg your pardon. Between a sniper rifle and any other kind of ordinary infantry small arms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the only difference -- yes, there was a difference. The difference was that it used special ammunition and had an optic sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose or the benefit of the optic sight was to the use of such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: With that kind of weapon, you could target at a distance. You could target specific objects which you had to see close to if you were to hit your target correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did that have on the effective range, therefore, of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: The person doing the shooting using this type of weapon could select his target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us any idea of the kind of distance, perhaps in metres, where that would be effective?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It could be effective up to 1.000 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also referred to having special ammunition. Can you say what was special about that ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It was special because the actual bullet contained lead. And it also had some other properties. But the ammunition was lead ammunition which inflicts greater injuries on the target, which means that it is high-precision targeting, and the wound inflicted would be greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having said that, can you tell us -- I'm not asking you to be any kind of ballistics expert here, Mr. Kovac, but can you tell us what they told you what was the difference therefore in how the lead bullets that you used in the sniper weapon differed from the bullets in a normal infantry weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: The success rate in targeting was much higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you recall what brand or make that that sniper weapon was that you were given?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: The sniper rifle was manufactured by the weapons factory of Kragujevac. It was a rifle of a 7.9 millimetre calibre. It was carbine, in fact, of the carbine type. So in addition to the fact that it was used as a carbine, it could also be used as a sniper rifle because the optic sight was placed on the carbine, turning it into a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other thing I would ask you about that: You refer to the optic sight. Can you tell us what make and type of thing that optic sight was.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: They were optic sights, domestically produced, probably. They were military domestic sights. I can't tell you the manufacturer's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the level of magnification that that sight was designated for?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. On the optic sight, when you looked through the optic sight itself, there was certain markings for distance so that there were certain distances on the optic sight, and you could determine with great precision how far you wanted to target objects, at what distance your targets were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac, when did you in fact complete your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: I completed my compulsory military service, that is to say, I went to the former Yugoslav people's army at the beginning of 1983, on the 7th of January, in fact. And I left the former Yugoslav people's army on the 28th or 29th, one of those two days, of November, 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what profession did you follow after you had left military service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: After doing my military service, I got a job in the Novi Grad municipality, and I dealt with civil defence matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the civil defence area of your career?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: In fact, from 1984, the beginning of 1984, right through to the present, I am in civil defence. I never interrupted my work -- years of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now then please tell the Chamber which positions you have held and where in your career in civil defence to date.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: At first, I was a coordinator for civil defence and monitoring training in civil defence among the population, that is, protection of the population in the municipality of Novi Grad. Then I was coordinator for protection and relief measures. And at the beginning of the war, that is at the beginning of 1992, I was appointed head of the civil defence staff for Novi Grad municipality. In 1994, the beginning of that year, I was appointed commander of the district staff of civil defence for Sarajevo. In 1995, I was appointed head of civil defence staff for the city of Sarajevo. In 1996, I was appointed head of the civil defence staff for the canton of Sarajevo, and that is the position I hold now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovac, if I can take you back to just before -- around the beginning of 1992, what sort of events had the Civil Protection force or civil defence been organised to deal with? What sort of ...

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, civil defence dealt with its activities which involved removal, evacuation, and care for casualties and people exposed to risk, without yet having any idea of what was to come. We, in the civil defence, kept the population informed of possible attacks on the city, or rather, to be more specific, the area of the municipality of Novi Grad. And we sought to organise life in such a way so that the civil population would overcome the situation as easily as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is a situation you faced, then, at the beginning of 1992. I should have perhaps asked this beforehand. What was the Civil Protection or civil defence set up for prior to that, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Civil defence in the former Yugoslavia was formed with a view to protecting and rescuing the population in jeopardy, or needing care. And it came under the defence secretariat. When talking about the components of defence in the former Yugoslavia, civil defence was a defence component, if I can put it in that way, intended to protect the civilian population, and that was its exclusive responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that description, what was the relationship or the intended relationship at that time between the civil defence and, let us say, the army, and the police, those three different bodies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: According to the laws formerly in force and prescribed at the level of the former Yugoslavia, the defence consisted of the armed forces, the civil defence, the system of information and reporting, and special purpose production. The armed component consisted of the army and the police, or rather, the present-day police. So civil defence was the unarmed component of defence, and its task was to defend the country, or rather to defend the population with the means available to it, to the civil defence, and that means with shovels, pick axes, fire extinguishing equipment, stretchers, medical teams, through units of civil defence that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So from whom in civil defence did you take any instructions to take action in Sarajevo when the conflict began in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: In our concrete case, we received instructions from the city staff of civil defence for Sarajevo, but the instructions certainly came from the republican level, civil defence staff, which operated at the level of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this republic staff was within the framework of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your Civilian Protection staff, how were they recruited and from what sectors of the population did they tend to come?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: If we're talking about recruitment to the staff of civil defence or protection at the beginning of 1992, then I can say that a large number of people was retained in the staff. A certain number of people left Sarajevo. And we filled in their places primarily with people who were by profession and by education capable of performing those tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've made reference to the start of the war in Sarajevo. Can you, very briefly, just describe the conditions that existed after May of 1992 and for the rest of that year, in terms of what actually happened, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: If we were to view it from the point of view of the civil defence, in that period, the civil defence had a lot to do. We had a large number of wounded and killed civilians. Also, we had a large number of refugees that had moved from certain parts of Sarajevo towards either the centre of town, that is, to certain municipalities, or through certain different channels left the country. And I can say that in the territory of Novi Grad municipality, in that time period, there was about 40.000 refugees from parts of Eastern Bosnia, parts of the municipalities of Ilidza, Novo Sarajevo, parts of the Vogosca and other areas swept by war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You've mentioned wounded and killed civilians. Can you describe how these people were being wounded and killed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, there were frequent shellings. The shellings usually were sudden or, on the other hand, continuous. When talking about the sudden shellings, shells would fall unexpectedly in a crowd where people had gathered for supplies, whether it be to receive humanitarian aid or to collect water, or places where various products were being sold or on sale, that is, at marketplaces. In addition, there were attacks on apartment buildings, and these buildings provided no safety for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you say roughly the areas around the city that received shells on any given occasion? Were there any particular areas that were targeted or was it more general?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It is hard to say that there were targeted areas. More or less every neighbourhood was shelled, some more, some less. But virtually every neighbourhood was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how regular was this shelling? Let's say through 1992 and even through 1993, how often did it occur?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: In the first year, that is, if we're talking about 1992, I can say that the shelling was very frequent. The pauses between the shellings were brief, and the shelling occurred either early in the morning, at dawn, and then it went on all day or it would start early in the evening and go on all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other kind of shooting that affected your life in Sarajevo while that war was on, other than the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the lulls when people would come out of their homes, along the routes that people took to town and back, various kinds of weapons were used to target them. At first, we didn't know what types of weapons and artillery were being used. But after a certain period of time, people learned that these were sniper bullets, that is, sniper shots, also machine-gun fire, so-called sowers of death, and then light anti-aircraft guns were also used, the so-called Pat, P-A-T, which at the top of the round are armoured, so that they could go through walls and destroy buildings and penetrate inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, faced with that situation, what were the first actual practical things that the civil defence were deployed to do? Did you have to have anything to do with the utilities or what other things did you do practically at the beginning of the war in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the conflict broke out, electricity was cut. Then water supplies were also interrupted, and there was major damage inflicted on the infrastructure. And what I mean is the PTT network, the water supply network, the sewerage, and in any event, it was our duty to organise ourselves and to try to do our best to ensure supplies for the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What action did your civil defence people take in respect of water supply? What was your involvement in that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: When we're talking about that problem, we organised -- or rather, through the town civil defence staff, we organised delivery of water with the help -- with the assistance of tank trucks, to all the municipalities. And all the local communities, through the civil defence, had a timetable for water delivery, and we took part in those deliveries so that water was transported every two or three days to a certain location, where people would be waiting in line. And in that way, they were supplied with water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the water come from in the first place that filled these trucks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Those were -- in those days, there were very few sources of water. There was water coming from the area of the brewery, which is in the old part of the city. And the Sarajevo brewery used to use that water to produce beer, and it still does, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of those deliveries, did these trucks ever encounter difficulties because of shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: In our plans of supplies, we sought to find locations that were better protected and that were not so visible. But nevertheless, it did happen that in some way unknown to me, those locations were shelled nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these arrangements for the water, did they carry on through 1993, throughout that year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the winter of 1993 to 1994, what were the conditions like for supplying water to the city in terms of the work your Civil Protection did? What were the conditions like for supplying the civilians with water?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Talking about winter, in addition to the water, which was an acute problem, another major problem was heating. I still remember very well the winter of 1992/1993. People sought various ways to come by firewood. They would even destroy their own furniture in their dwellings in order to heat the areas in which children lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
