utterances.text: Thank you. But if I may return to that question, Mr. Kovac, what about the supply of the water to the people during that winter of 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: So in addition to these tank trucks or trucks with reservoirs, pumps were also built in certain areas, and that was one way in which we improved the water supply. That is, in the parts of the municipalities where there was water in the ground and we received some water pumps from some humanitarian organisations, and we drilled for water and installed those pumps there and thus improved the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we," do you mean physically the staff of your own civil defence people? They were actually doing the work? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the similar situation for the electricity service to the city? Did your civil defence workers have an active physical role in anything to do with supply or repair for that particular resource, for electricity?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. With the help of professional teams coming from the electricity board of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of work, physical work, did that involve your staff doing in respect of the electricity supply?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they worked to dig, to protect the cables leading to transformer stations. And during the wartime, we resorted to cables along the ground so that canals had to be dug for those electricity lines because all the transmission lines on pillars were damaged, and even if they were repaired, they would be destroyed again, so that we decided to protect those cables by digging them into the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your people carry out this type of work throughout the conflict, that is, say, certainly from May 1992 up to the end of 1993, early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Mostly. With the assistance, I must say again, of the professionals from the electricity board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement with the other utility of town, the gas system? Did you ever have work to do on that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. And there was some natural gas, but to be quite frank, we couldn't rely on it on a more durable basis for fuel. Nevertheless, in the 1992/1993 period, a number of neighbourhoods, with the assistance of the civil defence, was provided with gas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the shelling and sniping going on whilst your people performed work on these utilities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout that time, there were shelling and other types of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Civil Protection service have anything to do with the issue of food for the city during that same period, during the conflict or the part of it from May 1992 up to the end of 1993, early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly. It was through the civil defence that food was distributed among all local communities and to all neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go about that? Did that require going to specific distribution points or taking food stuffs to individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: There were places in the local communities where the citizens that were mobile would come to those places. For citizens who were unable to move, the old, the weak, or sick, we organised delivery to their place of residence, to their place of homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the general way -- you say the citizens that were mobile would come to those places. Were these regular distribution places or did you alter those collection places from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Precisely for security reasons, we changed those distribution points precisely because of the possibility of them being shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this distribution by your people of locally-produced food stuff, i.e., food that was within Sarajevo, or was that involved in the distribution of outside humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't have asked you that cleverly to you, Mr. Kovac. Was that locally grown or locally produced food that you delivered?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Mostly, as there was insufficient food in 1992 and 1993 and later as well, then certainly it was food that arrived in Sarajevo through humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, did the civil defence have any other areas in which they tried to -- physically, to improve the survival lifestyle of the civilians? Did they, for instance, make any products that could be used? Were they involved in any things like clothing or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly. At the level of the city and also at the level of each Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the municipalities, we organised workshops, and all able-bodied people in the appropriate fields were recruited so that we had a workshop for the repair of roofs that were damaged through the shelling, and then these people from the civil defence would go and cover those buildings. We also had tailor shops, and all people who lacked clothing and footwear, we assisted them by making something for them to wear so they would be protected, especially during the winter months. We also had workshops for repairing the gas network, for repairing the electricity distribution system when there was electricity for brief periods, for repairing the PT network. The PTT did function, but then their experts worked in various neighbourhoods and monitored the functioning of the PTT network. And then there were also specialists and teams for repairing the electricity grids, though as I have said, electricity was in very short supply during this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as regards, you've mentioned helping to fix roofs. Were there any other areas of involvement that the Civil Protection had in connection with the damage to buildings as such?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. We repaired, that is to say, the UNHCR sent to our central warehouse at the level of the city staff, plastic foil arrived and other protective materials. And from them, they were distributed it to the local communities. And after that, teams went out to see to the repair work and protected windows with this plastic sheeting because the glass -- the windows had been shattered on many buildings. And this would make life easier for the people living inside. It would make it warmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of your own duties, did you have cause to go around the city of Sarajevo much, or did you stay mostly within your one municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It depended on the need. There were various meetings at the level of the municipality, and depending on where their office was. As for the Novi Grad municipality, I was in the field quite a lot. That is to say, I toured the local communities fairly frequently and moved around in the region I was in charge in, which was the Novi Grad municipality, mostly. I went into town only sporadically. And let me tell you, to be quite frank, the situation in Novi Grad was the same as in all the other parts of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms, having referred to damage to property, how bad was that damage in Novi Grad or the other areas that you toured around, let us say by the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: As I'm not an expert in the field in assessing damage, I can't tell you exactly what the damage to property was. I think the damage is enormous, and cannot be assessed. I think that the damage was extremely great and only expert reports and investigations done by professionals in the field could give a proper answer to that question. But at the level of the municipalities, commissions were set up to ascertain the damage done, and they functioned within the town planning departments. And after every shelling, those commissions, having been informed by the civil defence people that certain property had been damaged in a certain locality, those commissions, in keeping with the prevailing situation, would go out to that locality to ascertain what damage had been done. And I think that at the level of all the municipalities, and at the level of the city of Sarajevo itself, this has been calculated. It exists in figures. They have figures as to what the damage incurred was, and it was inestimable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like -- really suggest it was a case of your own naked eye. I would ask you one thing, was there any difference -- in the sense of buildings that were damaged or less damaged, was there any difference between domestic houses and apartment blocks and offices and other buildings in terms of them receiving some damage, or was everything?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: If we were to look at it that way, I don't think we could divide it up in that way. For example, that the target -- that what was targeted was office buildings or private buildings and so on. I think there was damage all over the place at one and the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's just one thing I would ask you. You say there were quantities of plastic delivered, the plastic foil for windows. Can you tell me, please, what colour that plastic was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: It was white, and it said the "UNHCR" on it in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, at that time while all this work was going on by your people in civil defence, how many people did you have in your civil defence force to do this work?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: On my staff, I had ten people, ten of my assistants. And they were my assistants in the different areas of rescue and protection work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of those assistants, did they or were they able to call upon the services of other people to perform work?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you indicate, in your municipality, how many people in all would have been working in Civil Protection during -- or civil defence, I'm sorry, civil defence during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: As far as the civil defence staff of the municipality is concerned, we had a total of 12 people working there. In the local communities, civil defence staffs of that particular local community were set up and they had five members each. In addition to those cadres, if I can call them that, there were civil defence units which were set up in 22 local communities in the Novi Grad municipality. Each of those units numbered approximately between 30 to 50 members. And in addition to those people, there were the civil defence foremen who informed and monitored 20 inhabitants in the area, were in charge of that many number. 200, I beg your pardon, 200 inhabitants. So that the figure -- if we look at 22 local communities times 30 persons on an average, that would make it about 600 people or 1.000 people working in the civil defence area for Novi Grad. The Novi Grad municipality at that time had 120.000 inhabitants, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kovac, what was the ethnic composition of your staff and then generally the civil defence people in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: I can say quite frankly and openly that the ethnic composition was satisfactory. When I say that it was satisfactory, I must say that some of the inhabitants of the Novi Grad municipality had left following certain directives; or for some other reasons, they had left the Novi Grad municipality. But many people stayed on as well. I was very pleased to see that quite a lot of people stayed, and this was reflected in the area of civil defence. In my own staff, out of the ten of us there, four people were the representatives of other nations. And if you like, I can give you their names and surnames. They were representatives of the Serbs, the Croats, and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, we've heard that there was a mobilisation during 1992, obviously to form the army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So where were you able, then, to draw your Civil Protection people, civil defence people, if a lot of young men and middle-aged men, presumably, went into the army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: When the mobilisation appeal was made, and in conformity with the instructions given out by the Defence Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, many people reported to the local communities and secretariats of defence in the municipalities in which they lived. Now, when it came to civil defence, some of the young people had applied to the civil defence to begin with. But very soon after afterwards, when these national -- when the defence secretariat was doing the mobilisation, sent those people to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the civil defence, it was mostly people over the age of 40 or 45 who stayed on. And there were also women and young people who were not fully capacitated to perform military duties, partially unfit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could move on to the relations between the civil defence forces of people and other services to the city. You mentioned earlier the question of moving population and evacuation. Is that right? You can just answer rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your civil defence people have anything to do with the ambulance service of the city?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what way did civil defence offer assistance to the ambulance service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the activities that the civil defence conducted within the local communities, we set up teams for first aid to people in the local areas. And those teams were able to give basic first aid. But we had also organised a certain number of vehicles so that the people who had been injured or were suffering in any way, we were able to transfer them to larger centres for -- where they were able to get medical assistance. So we took them to the hospitals, whether they were state hospitals or the Kosevo compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in organising those vehicles, did you do anything to try and distinguish them as ambulance-type vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the aim, and we placed a Red Cross symbol on those vehicles which denoted vehicles specifically intended for the transport of persons who were wounded or injured. But let me also mention in this regard that we used other vehicles, too, vehicles who happened to be at a certain place at a certain time. And in order to save citizens' lives, we had to intervene on an emergency basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether any of those marked vehicles that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deployed for this purpose ever sustained any kind of gunfire from either shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Even the ambulances, the official ambulances, belonging to the municipality, they were destroyed, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what manner? You say they were destroyed. In what way were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: When they were passing through certain danger zones in town, and also they were targeted by snipers on the one hand, and they were shelled on the other. Now, whether the shelling had targeted these vehicles on purpose or whether they were hit by chance, accidentally, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've made reference also to "the official ambulances belonging to the municipality." What kind of vehicles were they, and what kind of colours were they and markings did they have?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they were the classical type of vehicle. They were combi-vans, the kind that are used all over the world for ambulances, which means they were white vans with a Red Cross emblem on them, and it said "ambulance" on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of identifying lights on them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they had the sirens, blue lights on the roofs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your civil defence service have an involvement with the fire brigade or fighting fires?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. We had very good cooperation with the fire brigade of the city of Sarajevo, and let me say that at the beginning of the war, in all the municipalities, a specialised unit for extinguishing fires was set up for fire-fighting. And it functioned within the frameworks of voluntary fire-fighters associations. And as such, those units were added to the professional fire brigade for the city of Sarajevo, to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your staff members get involved in dealing with a lot of fires during the conflict period that I've referred to, from May 1992 up to the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. They were large-scale fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did -- what sort of equipment did your people have to try and tackle these fires compared, say to, the local fire brigade and such?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, we endeavoured to ensure that people could be recognised as fire-fighters in the fire-fighting society. In addition to the fire brigade, we had the necessary equipment and uniforms that the fire-fighters were able to avail themselves of. They had certain uniforms, not perhaps state of the art, but quite good enough. They had helmets which were usually yellow, and they also had hoses and a number of fire engines, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they have to perform -- sorry, I won't ask that. Thank you. What I would like to do is just ask you quickly as well -- I'm mindful of the time, Your Honours -- as to relations with the police. What were the different duties that the police would perform in the town and civil defence people would perform?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: By law, the law that was enforced at the time and the rules and regulations coming from the internal affairs ministry, and they were rules and regulations that were well known to the people at the head of the police force, the police dealt with security tasks, law and order within a settlement, and giving assistance to the army if there was an escalation of the conflict in certain regions or areas. As far as the civil defence's relations with the police are concerned, it was always a correct and proper relationship, and always within the frameworks of the laws in force at the time. Through our commissioners, our civil defence commissioners, and staffs in the local communities, we would supply the police with any information that could have been of interest for the police, and we were satisfied with that cooperation. And in certain cases, the police would help us if there was unrest when aid was being distributed or water was being distributed, and other situations as well which required the police -- which required the police assistance. Or if there was any general unrest in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any dealings yourself or any linked activity with the UN forces in Sarajevo, the UNPROFOR presence? Did you have any dealings with them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. And I should like to point out that we had some very fine cooperation. I had direct and continuous cooperation, in fact, and visits from the foreign legion's battalion, which was in charge of the Sarajevo airport and which following UN tasks had come to see what was going on in the Novi Grad municipality. So in addition to visiting the other services and organs, they would pay regular visits to the civil defence staff, the municipal civil defence staff and the local communities and staffs within those communities. So we had excellent cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, if I may interrupt you, if you could find a suitable moment within the next two or three minutes to finish at least for today your examination, I would be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I had one, I trust, brief question on this topic, and I was going to suggest to Your Honours we had found a very natural break in the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question I would like to ask you, Mr. Kovac, very quickly. Did you receive any assistance from the UNPROFOR from time to time, i.e. with actual equipment or actual physical help?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: From time to time they would assess the situation in places where people had -- where there were a lot of people, or in relation to ambulances, if they had a bit of fuel or a bit of food. Let me say that it wasn't under their competence to help us. We received aid from other channels, from other humanitarian organisations. But yes, the assistance they were able to give was always very welcome. So I can say that we had very good cooperation, and they were there to monitor and see whether the humanitarian aid was distributed properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That is very much a natural break, Your Honour, for my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. It is almost 7.00, so I would suggest that we adjourn now and resume by tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Ms. Pilipovic, I saw you almost standing up. Is there anything you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, then. The Court will sit in recess until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m. Thank you.
